AN OUTRAGE IN BARN- WELL.
A Witness in a Murder Case Kidnapped and Whipped on Account of his Testimony.
BLACKVILLE, August 9. — Cyrus David, a colored barber, was fooled into the country last night and given a severe flogging. A party went to his home and told him he was wanted to shave a dead man and he started out in the vehicle, but it came very near his being the dead man. A crocus sack was thrown over his head and a severe whipping administered. This morning he looked rather badly bruised. He says he was told that the reason he was whipped was because of his having given certain evidence against a party recently charged with murder in a case which attracted a great deal of interest. This evidence is alleged to have been given at the second trial in connection with the tragedy. The chief of police had heard of the incident, but no official report had been made to him and the whipping was done in the country.

It might not be hard work for the right persons to find out who committed this outrage and have the law take its proper course

Prohibitionist Nomination. VOORHEESVILLE, N. Y., Aug. 16.—The Prohibitionists of Albany county have nominated H. W. Elmendorf for Senator in the Twenty-ninth district. WHITE CAPS IN SOUTH CAROLINA. Inhuman Treatment of a Negro and a White Man and His Family.
CHARLESTON, S. C., Aug. 16.—The news from Barnwell county of the doings of the White Caps is interesting in view of the fact that arrangements are pending for the immigration of quite a number of settlers from Pullman, Ill., to that county. The news heretofore published of the white capping of Circus Davis, colored, on Thursday night last, and of George Carroll on Monday night, give but a meagre intimation of the real facts connected with these gross violations of the law.

The treatment of Davis was inhuman. He was not only badly whipped and beaten, but lighted matches were applied to his wounds, and he was left lying in the woods all night, where he was found the next morning and carried home. It is said that he was told that this severe punishment was inflicted upon him because he swore falsely in a certain case in the Court of Sessions in which he was a witness on the part of the State.

Monday night's outrage was the second time that the mob visited its displeasure upon George Carroll. They broke into his house, where he and his wife and children were asleep, smashing door and windows and breaking up Carroll's guns. They took him off from his home and beat and abused him outrageously, while some of them remained and kept his wife and children from following, and even struck his wife and little boy and choked his fourteen-year-old daughter because they undertook to aid the husband and father. Carroll is severely if not seriously injured.
This outrage business has been going on for more than a year in and about this same part of the county, and presumably by the same leaders. They make no distinction on account of race or color. Davis is a negro and Carroll and his family are white, and in their previous visitations they have oftener selected white victims than colored. There is no political feature involved in it. Thirty suspects have been arrested. Several claim that they can prove an alibi. The only crime charged against Carroll was that he was unsociable.

SOUTH CAROLINA.
Wednesday excursion trains out of Charleston for the North Carolina mountains carried 700 passengers.

D. A. J. Sullivan has gone to Rockville, where he will look after granite that is to be used in a new monument that is to be erected to John C. Calhoun in Charleston. It is to take the place of the one now in Marion square.

Columbia News: Jefferson May has been awarded the contract for repairing and renovating the inside work of the Columbia Female College, and to build their annex, the industrial hall. There were six bids, and Mr. May was successful at his bid of $5,000. This will be an improvement to the college, and will greatly widen its field or usefulness.

Columbia Corr. Charleston News: If the signs of the times count for aught the days of the constabulary force are counted. There is considerable talk about cutting the force down to a dozen or more select men and have them take in the state generally. It is thought that the constables generally are having very much of a "pie" time and that there is no use for the good done to keep up the force at its present cost of about $40,000 for the year.

Columbia News: Mrs. N. A. Martin, who lives a few miles from Ninety-Six, has kindly furnished two cannon to be sent to the Atlanta exposition. They have been in the possession of her family for almost 100 years, and were used during the revolutionary war at the old Star Fort at Cambridge. They are about three feet long, nine inches in diameter at the butt and five inches at the end. The bore is about three inches in diameter, and they each weigh about 100 pounds. They have been used as and and irons. No doubt they were set on fire with a pine knot, as they would be the most most convenient form in which to handle fire in those good old days. The arms on which they were mounted have been broken off.

Edward Cornish and Abraham Washington, two colored citizens, who are not worrying themselves about the constitutional convention, went out hunting hogs in the Congaree swamp the other day. They carried a gun and with that that hoped to capture a wandering hog. The hog came along and and Cornish fired at the animal. The hog was wounded and the negroes went after him, when some unknown third person came along, saw what was going on, picked up Cornish's gun, with which he fired at the hog, and banged away at the would-be thieves. Washington did not stop running until he reached home, and he is very much worried over the fact that that Cornish has not yet reported. He thinks that Cornish has not not yet reported. He thinks that Cornish has not been broken off.
A. H. Patterson of Barnwell was in Columbia Saturday. He spoke to Gov. Evans about the white-capping matter and stated positively that there's no organize band of white-caps in the county, and that the cases that have been reported each stand on their own bottom. The Nevils case, he said, occurred in about this manner: A colored boy was caught under a building looking at young girls. He was let off on the understanding that his parents should give him a good whipping. A brother of the inquisitive boy objected to the whipping being given by the parents of the boy, and interfered with the carrying out of the proceeding. Certain white persons went to see about the matter and being told of the interference of the brother took him out and gave him a whipping. Mr. Nevils, then, so it is said, took out warants against some of the white men who did the whipping, as he thinks that such treatment will influence the labor to leave his farm.

Charleston Sunday News: Friday morning, about 3 o'clock, as Detectives Miller and James Hogan were walking along Pitts street, near Montague, they saw a negro man run out of a gate and dodge behind a tree nearby. His actions were so suspicious that they immediately ordered him to surrender, assuring him that to run meant a coroner's jury case, and arrested him. SHOT WHILE PREACHING.
A Negro Minister Killed While Standing
in His Pulpit.
MITCHELL STATION Ala. July 29
Mitchell STATION, Ala., July 29. Sunday services were being conducted in a negro church near here when a pistol shot was fired and the preacher, Rev. Eli Williams fell dead in his pulpit. The ball entered his heart. Swing and Pleasant McKee, two negroes, who were standing outside, were arrested. They are held, however, simply as witnesses.
eli-williams-mitchell-station-1895-07-28.A2:
Shot the Preacher Dead.
MITCHELL STATION, W. Va., July 29.—Sunday services were being conducted in a Negro church near here, when a pistol shot rang out, and the preacher, Rev. W. E. Lewis, fell dead in his pulpit. The assassin is believed to have stood outside the church building at the time he fired. His identity is not known.

FLOOD IN OKLAHOMA. Arkansas River Doing Great Damage to Farm Property.
PERRY, O. T., July 30.—From parties arriving from the Arkansas river bottom it is learned that the river's overflow is doing great damage to low bottom farms along the river from Ponca City for 100 miles southeast.

Many fine fields of corn are now under water waist deep, and hundreds of acres have been washed away: The Osage Indians living in the bottoms on the north side have been compelled to move to higher ground. It is reported that the new bridge across the river at Blackburn has washed away.

ACCIDENT TO AN ATHLETE.

Impaled on a Vaulting Pole, Which Broke and Stuck In the Ground.

NEW YORK, July 30.—While practicing with the Bohemian Sokul Athletic club Joseph Petroneak met with a singular and probably fatal accident. He was making a high jump with a vaulting pole when it broke into three pieces. One of the middle sections entered the ground a few inches, and in falling Petroneak was impaled on the jagged end. The stick was forced through the ribs and penetrated the right lung. There is little hope of his recovery.

Suit Against Ben Butler's Estate.

BOSTON, July 30.—Judge Knowlton of the supreme judicial court has rendered a decision in the case of the holders of Colorado Cattle company's bonds to recover from the General B. F. Butler estate sums aggregating $219,000, on the ground of alleged deceit and fraud on the part of General Butler, who it is alleged by misrepresentation wrongfully gained possession of certain bonds. The phase of the case is the question of standing in equity of the plaintiffs of this state, whose claims amount to $55,-000. The decision gives them a right to go before the equity court and the cases will therefore be prosecuted.

Brakeman's Close Call.

SALEM, W. Va., July 30.—Baltimore and Ohio trains were delayed seven hours by a freight wreck near here. A brakeman was thrown 50 feet from a car over a fence into a creek without being seriously injured.

Shot In the Pulpit.

MITCHELL, Ala., July 30.—Eli Williams, pastor of a colored church near here, was shot dead in his pulpit. The shot was fired from the outside. There is no clew to the assassin.

Got an Increase.

READING, Pa., July 30.—The Reading Iron company's sheet mill employes, 350 in number, yesterday received 10 per cent advance in wages.

WESTERN CROPS.
Traffic Managers Declare They Will Keep the Roads Busy Twelve Months.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., July 29.—Traffic managers of the Western roads are busily engaged these days in estimating the prospective size of the forthcoming corn crop. It is believed by them that from information they have a conservative estimate is to give the states of Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas 800,000,000 bushels. Of this amount 300,000,000 is credited to Kansas, 225,-000,000 to Nebraska and the balance to Iowa. This is of corn alone, leaving as much other cereals to be moved to market. The amount of traffic which is looming into sight will certainly keep the roads busy for at least twelve months to come so traffic men figure

SILVER MEN CHOSEN.

Sound Money Democrats Make No Efforts to Capture Delegations.

St. Louis, Mo., July 29.—Free silver men had everything their own way in the primaries to elect delegates to the Democratic state convention at Pertle Springs, August 6. In twenty-seven of the twenty-eight wards in the city friends of the single gold standard laid down and allowed 16 to 1 Democrats to walk away with the delegations. Democratic conventions were held in a number of the counties of Missouri and delegates elected to the Pertle Springs convention. In no case, so far as reported, was there a contest made by the gold men. Silver men were in every case chosen.

ABUSED BY WHITECAPS.

Four Masked Men Tar and Feather a Baptist Minister.

WESTMORELAND. Kan., July 29.—At 11 o'clock last night four masked men took Rev. T. S. Rooks, the Baptist minister of this place, from his home, five miles in the country, and tarred and feathered him. They kicked and beat him in a brutal manner, and he is lying at a farmer's house outside the town in a critical condition. Mrs. Rooks went along with her husband and says she knows the White Caps. She will swear out warrants for them. Excitement over the affair runs high. He was accused of trying to assault a young woman.

FOR EMBEZZLEMENT.

Ex-Banker Levy of Wichita Arrested on Charges of Robbing Wards.

WICHITA, Kan., July 29.—M. W. Levy of St. Louis was arrested quietly Saturday on a charge of embezzlement. He formerly lived in this city and was president of the Wichita National bank, receiver for numerous institutions and administrator of nearly thirty different estates. The complaint charges him with having embezzled $827 belonging to Walter W. Hays and Roy Mays, of whom he was custodian. He was released on $2,000 bail.

Helped Out By the Syndicate.

NEW YORK, July 30.—It is announced that on Friday last the government bond syndicate deposited with the subtreasury $2,000,000 in gold in exchange for legal tenders. This was done for the purpose of making good to the treasury the amount of gold withdrawn by various persons for shipments to Europe and other places during the month. This deposit brings the government gold balance up to the highest point reached since the syndicate has completed its payments on account of bonds.

Assassinated in the Pulpit.

MITCHELL STATION, Ala., July 30—Services were being conducted in a negro church near here Sunday, when the report of a pistol rang out and the preacher, Eli Williams, fell dead in his pulpit, a ball having entered his heart. The assassin is believed to have stood outside the church building at the time he fired. His identity is not known. Swing and Pleasant McKee, two negroes, who were standing outside were arrested. They were simply held as witnesses, however.

More People for Missouri.

SEDALIA, Mo., July 30.—A movement has been inaugurated here to make the "Missouri on Wheels" project a permanent institution, with a view of increasing the wealth and population of the state 25 per cent by 1900. The proposition is to secure 100,000 Missourians to contribute $1 each per annum for the purpose of attracting capital and immigration to Missouri. In furtherance of the scheme, a convention will be held late this fall to perfect a state organization.

A Woman Horsethief Caught.

JOPLIN, Mo., July 29.—A few days ago a strange woman came here with a team and buggy and offered them for sale. She was arrested on suspicion of horse stealing. Yesterday telegrams from Caldwell, Kan., described a woman and team closely corresponding with these and requested that she be arrested. The authorities of Caldwell were notified and an officer is expected here this evening.

WILL BE LYNCHED.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 14.---Mrs. Hutchings, wife of a prominent tobacco dealer, with grown-up family, was raped by a negro three miles from here. The negro is surrounded by a posse, and will undoubtedly be lynched. Mrs. Hutchings is in a critical condition, and is not expected to recover from the shock.
harp-alias-mud-danbefand-lexington-1895-.A2:
A Negro's Life in Danger.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 14.—To-day Mrs. Hudson was assaulted by a negro near this city. Her screams attracted the attention of men working in the field near by. The negro escaped before they arrived. The neighbors scoured the fields all day in search of the negro. Blood hounds were put on the trail to-night and a negro named Harp, alias Mud Danberand, was caught at midnight. Mrs. Hudson is highly connected and is in a serious condition. If she identifies Harp to-morrow as the guilty person it is generally believed he will be lynched.
harp-alias-mud-danbefand-lexington-1895-.A5:
A WOMAN'S ASSAILANT
Surrounded in a Corn Field, and Will Be Captured by Bloodhounds.

LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 15. ---Wednesday morning an unknown Negro entered the home of Mrs. Hutchings, living on the farm of Walter Payne, three miles from Lexington, and assaulted her. Her screams attracted the attention of men working in a tobacco field near by, and at their approach the fiend fled out of the house the back way, going into a corn field, which was quickly surrounded by neighbors of the woman.

Mrs. Hutchings was found in an unconscious condition with bruises on her throat and head. Word was quickly sent to the city, asking the aid of the bloodhounds and officials. County Judge Frank A. Bullock, Deputy Sheriffs Rogers and Bosworth, with several other men, went to the scene at once and the bloodhounds, which are at the house of 'Squire Levi Grow, in the country, have been sent for in a hurry.
harp-alias-mud-danbefand-lexington-1895-.A10:
SMITH IDENTIFIED. Two Witnesses Say That He Was Near the Scene of Mrs. Hudson's Assault.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 16.—Jas. Hogan, a section hand on the Louisville Southern, Thursday afternoon identified Henry Mitchell Smith, the Negro charged with assaulting Mrs. Hudson, as the man he saw near the scene of the crime a short time before it was committed. Molly Miller, a colored woman who gave the same Negro a drink of water, positively identified Smith. The identification is considered so complete that Elijah and John Hudson, sons of the old lady, said that they intended to come to the jail Thursday night with one hundred and fifty armed men and lynch Smith. Chief of Police McElroy says there is no danger of a mob.
harp-alias-mud-danbefand-lexington-1895-.A13:
PROSPECTIVE LYNCHING.
Negro Ravisher's Life Periled by a Mob of Kentuckians.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 16.—There were never such scenes in this place as were witnessed to-night. Last Wednesday Mrs. Mary Hudson, white, wife of a prominent farmer, was outraged three miles from this city by a negro. The woman's screams attracted the men from the fields. They found Mrs. Hudson unconscious and the negro had fled. The country was scoured by hundreds of armed men and blood-hounds, and that night Henry Mitchell Smith was caught. He has been in jail here since. This afternoon Mrs. Hudson was brought to this city. She is still prostrated, but has recovered consciousness, and at 6 p. m. to-night positively identified Smith at the jail as her assailant. This caused great excitement, and Judge Bullock at once issued the following order and gave mandatory instructions for its most careful execution:

"It being the opinion of the judge of this court that the safekeeping of Henry Mitchell Smith, who is now in the jail of Fayette county, confined under a charge of having committed a felony, requires that a guard shall be kept over said Smith, it is now ordered that fifteen men be summoned to act as such guards, and that such men who are so to act be summoned by W. B. Wilkerson, deputy jailor of Fayette county, and that they be placed under the control of the said Wilkerson."

IS IT A RUSE?
UGTON Ky Aug 1
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 17, 1:20 a.m.—The jail is still heavily guarded. A big crowd is hovering around, waiting for the expected mob from the country. Two men just arrived from the neighborhood of the crime say the people have all gone to bed. These two only were sent out to watch the movements and hurry back and notify the jail authorities in case of mob preparations. They report the people expect to let the law take its course. This is thought to be a ruse, and it is feared an effort will be made to take the negro from the court room at the examining trial in the morning. A strong guard will be established at the court room, and all who enter will be searched for concealed weapons. If the mob appears during the trial it is believed they will succeed in getting their man.

Sentenced to Death. LEXINGTON, Ky., Sept. 21.—Henry Mitchell was sentenced to hang in this city for assaulting Mrs. Hudson a month ago. This is the second Negro to receive the death sentence at this term of court. Dick Suter Goes Up for Life.
TRANKFORT, Ky., Sept. 21.—The jury in the case of Richard Suter, for killing Harry Kelly, returned a verdict of life imprisonment, after being out two days and nights.

Kicked in the Face by a Horse.

McKINNEY, Ky., Sept. 21.—S. M. Owens, ex-judge of this county, was kicked in the face by a horse Friday, and received what is thought to be a very serious wound.

Stricken With Apoplexy.

CARROLLTON, Ky., Sept. 21.—Samuel Craig, a farmer, was stricken with apoplexy Friday and died instantly. Henry Young, aged 28, died of neuralgia of the heart.

To贺 Moonskinbrs.

MIDDLEBORO, Ky., Sept. 21.—United States deputy marshals and several officers of this city left Friday night for Harlan county to raid illicit distilleries.

Thrown From a Horse.

McKINNEY, Ky., Sept. 21.—Miss Nannie Reynolds was Friday morning thrown from a horse and received probably fatal injuries.

New Post Office in Kentucky.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 21.—A post office has been established at Neosheo, Ky., and William C. Yates appointed postmaster.

hartman-hartman-1895-08-01.A1:
IT WILL BE ALL OVER
If the Injured Child Identifies Him as the Fiend.
Chattanooga, Aug. 4.--The 12-year-old daughter of James Redwhite, a farmer living near Harriman, Tenn., was outraged by an unknown negro while on her way from Sunday school today. The negro met the girl in the road and threatened her with death if she made an outcry, dragged her into the bushes and assaulted her. The villain escaped before the girl could inform her friends, but the neighborhood is alive with searching parties, and if captured he will be lynched at once. An officer with blood-hounds left Chattanooga for Harriman tonight to assist in the search. Late tonight two negroes were arrested, one of whom is believed to be the right party. If the child identifies him it will be all over with him shortly.
hartman-hartman-1895-08-01.A5:
Hounds Chasing a Negro.
Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn., August 6.—Telegrams have been received from Harriman by Chief of Police Hill calling for the three bloodhounds, to be used in hunting for the negro who cruelly assaulted Miss Rex near that city Sunday. The greatest excitement prevails in Rome county, and the citizens of Harriman are threatening a lynching should he be captured. Officer Smith of the local police department left with the hounds.
hartman-hartman-1895-08-01.A6:
BLOODHOUNDS ON THE TRAIL.
A Small White Girl Assaulted by a Negro Near Harriman.
Chattanooga, Tenn., Aug. 6.—Bloodhounds are now on the trail of ravisher of 12-year-old Myrtle Rex, who was so cruelly outraged two miles from Harriman Sunday, while returning from Sunday school. The negro is thought to have gone in the direction of Lenoir, Tenn. The town has resumed its former quiet, and the talk of lynching has ceased.
hartman-hartman-1895-08-01.A8:

The negro who assaulted the 12-year-old daughter of James Red, at Harriman, Tenn., will be lynched if caught.

Joseph Winger has been arrested at Astoria, Ore., for obtaining money by representing himself as the Bishop of Honolulu.

West Superior, Mtch., is being ruled by two mayors—the president of the common council and the recently-impeached mayor.

CHILD BRUTALLY OUTRAGED.
A Little Girl, Formerly of Steubenville Terribly Mistreated in Tennessee.
Special to the Register.
A Little Girl, Formerly of Steubenville Terribly Mistreated in Tennessee.
Special to the Register.
Steubenville, O., Aug. 7.—The following about a family that moved to Harreman, Tenn., several years ago, from this county, has reached this city: Great excitement exists in the community over the flendish and brutal outrage of a twelve-year old white girl yesterday by a negro twenty years of age. The child is a daughter of Darwin Rex, a farmer recently moved from Ohio. He has two daughters, pretty, innocent, girls. The girl assaulted was the younger and a very delicate child. She was returning to her home from Sunday School, when she was stopped in the road by a negro youth. Frightened at his words the little girl turned and ran, but the negro caught up with her in a short distance, and seizing her around the waist with the left arm he put his right over her mouth to stop her screams and dragged her into the woods where he assaulted her twice and left her unconscious. When she regained her senses she dragged herself home and told her story, fainting in her mother's arms. The father and neighbors quickly armed themselves and started in pursuit, and a lynching will take place if he is caught.

Missoula, Aug. 9.—John Bonner and I. T. Hosey, representing the board of trade, accompanied by Ed Fowler and a Standard reporter, drove up over the Lou Lou grade this morning to examine the road, which has caused so much trouble in past years, and which it is desired to improve, if the county commissioners will consent. As is generally known, there are three "dug roads" or cuts along the steep sidehill beyond the Buckhouse bridge, all of which are inconvenient for travelers and at least two of which are positively dangerous. At no point on any of the three cuts can a loaded wagon be passed, and there are but one or two places where two light rigs can pass each other.

Nearly everybody who travels these roads with any frequency has had the experience of unhitching his horse, leading him up the sidehill and then running his buggy over the grade and holding it while a heavily loaded wagon passed. It is an experience which does not tend to make travelers appreciate the road, and it is no wonder that those who are obliged to drive over the grade want it improved. Until last year it has been possible to haul heavy loads over a lower road by fording the Bitter Root below the Mills ranch, but the high water last summer destroyed the ford and now all heavy teaming must be done over the grade.

The road along these three grades needs widening at least four feet. This is especially necessary in the case of the first two cuts, as in each instance the road is built around the point of a hill and one end of the road is hidden from the other. It is impossible for a man driving up on one end of the grade to tell whether there is a team coming the other way or not, and the hill drops abruptly from the road, a distance of 75 to 125 feet. In regard to the third cut, which is a long one, the same may be said. The road is very narrow, and the length of the cut in this instance makes it impossible to tell whether or not a team is approaching.

Additional danger exists in the loose earth and shell rock which are continually sliding down and blocking the road. These slides are small and are generally caused by horses and cattle grazing on the hill, above the road. This danger could be removed by the construction of a guard fence on the hill above the road.

The cost of the desired improvements in this road would not be great. There is no piece of road in the county that is used more than this, and the growing popularity of the springs up the Lou Lou are increasing the travel in this direction. The completion of the new Ravalli county bridge at Florence will also divert no small part of the business of that section to Missoula. The road this year is in good condition, comparatively speaking, but Supervisor Andrews cannot make a good road out of it until some improvements are made along the grade.

The county commissioners meet next Monday, and this matter will be brought to their attention. Messrs. Marion, Rankin and Deschamps will probably drive out to the grade during the next week and examine it for themselves.

A RAPIST CAUGHT.
Caught in Atlanta, He Is to Go to Tennessee for Trial.
Atlanta, Aug. 12.—Milton Dother, a negro wanted in Harriman, Tenn., for criminally assaulting a 14-year-old white girl, was arrested here this afternoon. He was followed from Harriman by Marshal Long and a deputy who has been on his trail for two weeks. They arrived in Atlanta to-day and identified the negro in a squad at work on the exposition grounds. He was put under arrest and will be taken back to Tennessee to-morrow. Marshal Long is afraid that an attempt will be made to lynch the negro, as the assault created great excitement in the town.
hartman-hartman-1895-08-01.A13:
ALMOST SURE TO SWING.
A Mob Said to Be on the Way to Take Gather, the Rape Fiend, From Jail.
New Orleans, Aug. 13.—A special to the States from Chattanooga says:

Last night George Gather, the negro rapist who outraged the young daughter of H. M. Rex, a leading citizen of Harriman, Tenn., who a week ago was caught in Atlanta by Detective Bern of that city, was returned to Chattanooga for transfer to Harriman, the scene of the rape.

The detective left here with his prisoner on the early train, and word was received at 11 o'clock that he arrived safely within three miles of the city and was met at the train by the sheriff, who took charge of the prisoner. Excitement is at fever heat and lynching is sure today.

Gather met Myrtle Rex, 9 years old, in the woods about a mile from her home and asked her to show him the home of a certain negro. She had been raised in the north to believe in negro virtue, and suspected no trouble when she consented. Near the house to which he asked to be directed he stopped and forced her to lie down. Accomplishing his purpose twice, the fiend escaped. Bloodhounds were put on the trail, but with no good result. Excitement has continued at fever heat, and it is now rumored that a posse is on the way to take Gather out and lynch him.

Girl Fails to Identify Him.
Knoxville, Tenn., Aug. 14.—George Gaither, the negro arrested in Atlanta, Ga., Monday on suspicion of being the assailant of Myrtle Rex, a 12-year-old girl of Harriman, was released this morning. The girl failed to identify him. Nearly fifty negroes have been arrested on suspicion since the crime was committed.

NEGROES DRIVEN OUT.
Whitecaps Cause an Exodus From a Texas County.
Whitecaps Cause an Exodus From a Texas County.

PARIS, Tex., Aug. 5.—News has reached here of a bad state of affairs prevailing in Delta County, which adjoins this (Lampas) County on the south. One night last week every negro was notified to leave the county at once, or he would be taken out and hanged. Notices were posted informing white men who undertook to protect them that they would meet with the same fate.

This caused a perfect stampede among the negroes, who, being thoroughly alarmed, began to move out of the county at once, although the good citizens tried to dissuade them and offered them every protection. In a radius of five miles 2000 acres of land, crops and all, were abandoned, and contracts for another year abruptly canceled. The whitecappers, or whoever they were, continued to post threatening notices, and the exodus has been complete.

Some negroes who owned valuable farms have remained behind to sell their lands for whatever they could get for them. There is great excitement over the outrage. Thousands of acres of the finest farming lands in the South will be idle in consequence.
william-stephens-pacio-1895-08-11.A2:
NEGRO CHURCH BURNED.
Lamar County Being Molested by Gangs of White Caps.
Paris, Tex., Aug. 9.—(Special.)—White Caps have invaded this county. Last night the negro church at the village of Glory, ten miles south of the city, was burned and notices posted ordering all negroes to get out of the country within ten days, with the significant suggestion that Winchesters would be used to move them if the demand was not complied with. Several negroes of this city received similar notices, and great consternation prevails among the colored people. Several negro families were driven from Delta county last week and took refuge here. The officers have not the slightest suspicion as to who are the investigators of the White Cap movement.
william-stephens-pacio-1895-08-11.A3:
BROTHERS QUARREL AND ONE IS KILLED NEAR LEXINGTON.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 12.—At Payne's Depot this morning Wesley Brock shot and killed his brother-in-law, Lewis Payne. The trouble originated over a pocket knife which Brock accused Payne of having taken. They quarrelled at breakfast. Payne jumped up and ran into the room where Brock's rifle was hanging on the wall. He took the gun down, but as he did so his sister, who is Brock's wife, grabbed him and tried to persuade him not to shoot her husband.

By this time Brock had come into the room, and, running up to the window, on the sill of which he kept his pistol, he picked up the weapon and fired one shot at his brother-in-law. The bullet struck him below the left shoulder blade and penetrated the heart. The wounded man ran out of the house, and fell fifteen steps from the door, leaving the rifle in the hands of his sister.

Brock assisted in carrying the body back to the house, testified before the Coroners' Jury, and surrendered himself to the Sheriff of Scott county, who placed him in jail. He says he fired in self-defense, and firmly believes that Payne would have killed him.

Sam Burke, a farmer, who lives near Pinkard, Woodford county, shot and mortally wounded his brother Frank late yesterday afternoon. Several months ago their mother died at Sam's house, and, being unable to send her body back to Rock Castle county, her former home, for burial, he had it interred at Pinkard. This angered Frank and his brother Morgan. Yesterday they got drunk on beer. Frank told Sam he intended to whip him for not sending his mother's body home, and that Morgan would whip him to-day. Sam replied that they had better keep their hands off him.

Frank ran into the house and got his pistol, came on to the porch, and began firing at Sam. Sam ran into the house by the back door, grabbed his shotgun, and fired at his brother as he came in the front door. The charge took effect in the right side and hip. Doctors say he will die. Sam Burke came to Lexington this morning carrying his shotgun to protect himself, he said, from his brother Morgan. He has not been arrested. He is 45. Frank is 25.

PITTSBURGH, Aug. 12.—Late on Saturday night Patrick and Dennis Morgan, brothers, employed in the Laurel Hill mines of W. P. Rend & Co., became involved in a quarrel. A crowd of miners were drinking beer, when the brothers disagreed over some trivial matters. Their companions, wishing some excitement, made no effort to separate them, and for fully twenty minutes the brothers slashed each other with their knives. Patrick was stabbed through the heart and Dennis will die of his wounds. Patrick was 26 years of age and Dennis is about 23.

DETROIT, Aug. 12.—Mrs. William Hass left her husband a week ago because of his abuse of her, and went back to her parents' home to live. This morning Haas walked into the kitchen where his wife and children and her father, Michael Kreig, were sitting.

"Are you going to live with me?" he asked.

"No," replied his wife.

Then Haas drew a revolver. Mrs. Haas picked up her baby and ran into another room, shutting the door behind her. Haas attempted to follow her, Kreig interfered, and Haas fired two shots at him, one taking effect in the left breast, just above the heart and the other passing clear through the left shoulder. Kreig will probably die. Haas was arrested.

CORSICANA, Tex., Aug. 12.—Scott Davis was instantly killed and Ellen Davis mortally wounded to-day by Albert Coleman. Coleman and Davis were friends of the Davis woman, and jealousy was the cause of the killing. Coleman was arrested.

PARIS, Tex., Aug. 12.—William Stevens, a thrifty negro farmer near Pacio, Delta county, who received a White Cap notice to leave and failed to obey it, was called to his door last night and shot dead.

PUEBLO, Col., Aug. 12.—Iza Dooley, who came here a year ago from Nebraska, shot her lover, James E. Doyle, in the shoulder last night, and then made an unsuccessful attempt to kill herself. Doyle's injury is not mortal, but the woman is in a precarious condition. Doyle told Miss Dooley that he was going to Denver, but could not take her with him.

SHELBY, Ia., Aug. 12.—Mrs. Wilhelm Kruger, wife of a prosperous farmer near here, was shot and beaten to death last night by her nephew, Herman Kohaupt, a young man 18 years of age, who has been working as hired man for the Krugers. Kohaupt then went to a neighboring cornfield, where he cut his throat with a razor, inflicting a wound which must have resulted in almost immediate death. Mr. Kruger, who was away at the time, says that Kohaupt came to him last March from Germany, and has been with him ever since. He was a morose, surly fellow, and for some reason never liked Mrs. Kruger.

ALBANY, Ga., Aug. 12.—Last Friday afternoon John Harris, 18 years old, a negro boy, went to the house of Mrs. John Monroe, a highly respectable white woman, aged 65 years, who lived near Hurbfield Hill. After choking her into insensibility he outraged her. Mrs. Monroe died a few hours afterward, but before dying regained consciousness long enough to tell who her assailant was. While Harris was committing the crime the screams of his victim were heard by some neighbors, who arrived in time to see him leave the premises. Being well known, his identification was complete and the alarm soon spread. A posse of 200 men was soon in hot pursuit. He was captured near Camilla Saturday andynched.

WILMOT, S. D., Aug. 12.—Dr. J. H. Whitford of this city, while temporarily insane, yesterday shot and killed his wife and then ended his own life. He had been a prominent physician here for many years.

KALAMAZOO, Mich., Aug. 12.—Simon and Edward Kastead, father and son, were frightfully hacked and stabbed by William Rose, a negro, in this city late Saturday night while they were trying to protect three girls whom Rose was trying to overtake on a lonely street. The Father had part of the muscles of one arm severed and received a thrust over the heart, and the son received a bad gash in the neck and several deep thrusts in the body. The girls had taken refuge from the negro in the Kasteads' ward, and the two men were attacked when they ordered him to leave. Rose was arrested this morning. His victims will probably be crippled for life.

NEW HAVEN, Aug. 12.—John Cisco, a colored man, made a murderous attack on a half-breed Indian named Ulysses Gaant Mason at West Haven last night, cutting him in a frightful manner. The weapon used was a razor. In the courthouse Court this morning Cisco was held to await the result of Mason's injuries. The trouble arose from a dispute over a game of cards.

ROSLYN, Wash., Aug. 12.—Superintendent George Harrison of the Northern Pacific Railroad's mines and George Blunt, a prominent miner, were drowned yesterday in Lake Cleelum, in sight of their families, 500 feet from shore. A storm came up suddenly, capsizing their boat. Would-be rescuers were nearly drowned.

ELWOOD, Ind., Aug. 12.—J. L. Henry, aged twenty, a Metropolitan Insurance agent who came here from Boston, Ind., a year ago, and lived with his mother, was found dead last night hanging by a rope to a transom, having been dead several hours. Some evidence indicates foul play. Henry was heavily insured on the company of which he was an agent. The rope was slack when he was found and he was on his knees. A handkerchief had been tied around his neck under the noose.

WHEELING, W. Va., Aug. 12.—Engineer Clemens C. Arns was killed and eight cars and one engine demolished in a freight wreck on the Baltimore and Ohio at Campon, twenty miles south of here, last night. WORK OF THE WHITE CAPS.
They Cause a Reign of Terror Among Negroes in Delta County, Tex.
One Farmer Who Failed to Leave Was Murdered in the Presence of His Mother.
PARIS, Tex., Aug. 12.—The White Caps were not satisfied with causing a reign of terror among the negroes of Delta County and their operations were extended to this county. The negroes were driven from Delta County almost to a man, and were notified to leave their homes and crops. The negroes from this county had commenced to flee when one of their churches was burned a few nights ago.

Negroes residing in the city have received notice to leave on peril of their lives. An aged negress reached here to-day and stated that her son, residing near Pacic in Delta County, was called to his door at 4 o'clock Saturday morning and shot down by the White Caps. His ten days' notice had just expired. He did not comply with the demand, for had he done so his crop would have been lost and the lives of the members of his family placed in jeopardy. His name was William Stephen and he was murdered in the presence of his wife, mother and children. He tried to sell out his crop, but could find no purchaser. The notice ordering him to leave was posted on his door. His brother is in hiding here.

Indignation is at red heat and more murders by these outlaws are expected. The negroes to-day issued an appeal through the press for protection. This lawlessness is not countenanced by the whites generally and every effort is being made to subdue it both by officials and citizens. Three arrests have been made to date. An evening paper says editorially:

"The officers of these two counties should make every effort to bring every one of these lawless gangs to speedy and severe justice. The penitentiary or the gallows is the place for all such characters. Not only the officers but the the people of the sections where White Cappers have broken out should arm themselves and pump lead into every White Cap found posting notices or doing other unlawful acts. Such outlawing must be suppressed, and if necessary the people should meet and use force. The end is not yet. More trouble is imminent and bloodshed may become general."

SHOT BY WHITE CAPS
ASSASSINS MAKING WAR ON NE- GROES IN DELTA COUNTY, TEXAS.
One Killed Because He Didn't Leave When Notified—North Carolina Blacks Fired on by Whites.

william-stephens-pacio-1895-08-11.A10:
WHITECAPS BREAK DOWN.
While on the Witness-Stand They Were Compelled to Confess.
Three Citizens of Texas Who Terrorized Negroes Fled for Their Lives.
PARIS, TEXAS, Aug. 13.—Finally the strong arm of the law has been invoked and is apparently proving as great a terror to the whitecappers of this county as they were to the negroes. Whitecapism in this county has been, it is thought, successfully nipped in the bud.

The Call correspondent has just returned from Glory, where Justice Yancey to-day held an inquest to determine whether whitecaps burned the colored church at that place, as charged, last Thursday night. The evidence was almost conclusively in the affirmative. It seems that one Hinson came into the Glory neighborhood some two weeks ago from Delta County, where the whitecaps held full sway, and proceeded to organize in this county among the illiterate young farmhands. He was in a measure successful. The usual notices were posted and the exodus began among the negroes.

Thursday night the negro church was burned and this aroused the whites. Among the witnesses at the inquest to-day was one Will Sheppard, who appeared quite nervous. He was asked to write one of the whitecap notices from dictation, and his production was almost identical with those posted on the negroes' door. His evidence was contradictory. He was placed under the rule and another witness called, when it was discovered that Sheppard had fled.

At this stage of the proceedings George Kitchen, another one of the gang, broke completely down and made a complete confession. He said it was previously agreed between them to burn the church and that they and others had printed the notices in this county. He also said that Sheppard was a member of the gang of Delta County. A warrant has been issued for the arrest of Hinson. Kitchen is in custody and officers are in pursuit of Sheppard. Indignation is running high among the whites and a lynching may follow. The jury at the inquest found that the Edora colored church had been burned by the three whitecaps named. The negroes are becoming quiet since the whites have taken such a decided stand looking to their protection.
william-stephens-pacio-1895-08-11.A11:
RATS INVADE AN ISLAND.
Inhabitants Compelled to Fly Before an Army of Hungry Rodents.
Many People Bitten and Every Vestige of Vegetation Destroyed by the Invaders.
TITUSVILLE, FLA., Aug. 14.—The island of Tropic, twenty miles south of here, has been invaded by an army of savage rats, and the inhabitants have been forced to flee for their lives.

Tropic is three miles long and two miles wide, and the soil is very fertile. A dozen families have settled on the island and engaged in growing vegetables for market. George Butler, one of the settlers, has just reached here, and tells a thrilling tale of the invasion and subjugation of Tropic by the rats.

Up to a month ago, according to Butler, there were no rats on the island. At that time the advance guard of the rodents arrived, and were quickly followed by others, until in two weeks there were fully 10,000 on the island. The rats came from the mainland, which is only two miles away, and Butler says that they swam across. He says he has seen them coming out of the water by hundreds.

At first the rats contented themselves with attacks on the vegetables, which were soon destroyed. Then they invaded the homes of the settlers. The latter made war on them, killing them by hundreds. Butler says that he has killed as many as a hundred without a stop, but that others would rush forward and attack him, biting him viciously on the legs.

In spite of the slaughter the rats got into the houses and attacked the women and children. Several of the latter were badly torn by the sharp fangs of the rodents. One baby was so severely bitten about the face that its life is despaired of. For three nights not a soul on the island slept, as that would have meant death.

At last the people in terror and worn out fled in their boats to the mainland, where they are now encamped in a destitute condition. The rats pursued them to the water's edge and the women and children were repeatedly bitten before the boats could be pushed off. Every vestige of vegetation has been destroyed on the island and it resembles a desert. The rats are described as gray in color and monstrous in size, being larger than squirrels.

WHITECAP LEADERS CAPTURED.

Sheppard and Hinson Placed Behind the Bars.

PARIS, Tex., Aug. 14.—Two more important whitecap arrests have been made since last night. Will Sheppard and Rube Hinson, both of whom were implicated by the confession of Kitchen, as chronicled in the dispatches of last night, are now safely behind the bars.

Sheppard was caught while endeavoring to leave the country at a rapid pace. He was heavily armed, but was taken by surprise. Hinson, the organizer and ringleader of the gang in this county, was also taken in a like manner. Federal authorities today decided to take a hand in the situation, and a force of Deputy Marshals will scour the country and run the gang down to a man.

Kitchen trembled like a leaf when making his confession when he described the oath administered to members. The penalty for divulging any of the secrets of the gang was death. The situation is more peaceful and the negroes are becoming somewhat quieted again. No news from the seat of trouble in Delta County was received to-day.

RAID BY WHITECAPS
ARE AFTER THE NEGROES OF DELTA COUNTY.
Large Number of Colored People Are Leaving Their Homes-One Man Has Been Killed.
Paris, Tex., Aug. 23.—(Special.)—A gentleman who has just completed a tour of Delta county arrived in the city today, bringing news of fresh outrages committed by the white caps in the last few days. Night before last he counted sixty men armed with winchesters and shot guns pass the house where he was stopping. Some wore the most hideous disguises and their ghostly appearances were calculated to terrify the stoutest hearted. Every negro has left the county, not waiting to sell their lands or crops. On Wednesday night, Jeff Cole, an aged and inoffensive negro, was called out of his house and riddled with bullets. He had been notified to leave the county in ten days, but his white neighbors advised him to stay, giving it as their opinion that there was no danger. Cole owned land and was in good circumstances. His family left next day, without waiting to bury him. White men who have tried to protect the negroes are being warned to leave, and great uneasiness prevails less a number of assassinations should take place.
